slides.title: Stop *junk* in SE11 with *fixed values*
slides.voiceover: Stop junk values in SE11 with zero code. Last time we learned Output Characteristics. Now, fixed values.
slides.spoken: Stop junk values in SE11 with zero code. Last time we learned Output Characteristics. Now, fixed values.

slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.heading: Status field, *no list*
slides.title: Table ZORDERS
slides.voiceover: Here's the problem. A status field without a list takes anything. Open orders, closed orders, then X, then ok. Nobody knows what X means.
slides.spoken: Here's the problem. A status field without a list takes anything. Open orders, closed orders, then X, then ok. Nobody knows what X means.

slides.heading: *Single* values
slides.note: Single Vals: Fix. Val. + Short Descript.
slides.voiceover: A fixed value is one allowed value. It comes with a short text. In SE11, pick your domain in change mode. Go to the Value Range tab, to Single Vals. First, O for open. Next, C for closed. Last, R for rejected. Then activate, and you are done.
slides.spoken: A fixed value is one allowed value. It comes with a short text. In SE11, pick your domain in change mode. Go to the Value Range tab, to Single Vals. First, O for open. Next, C for closed. Last, R for rejected. Then activate, and you are done.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: F4 shows the *list*
slides.title: Status: possible values
slides.voiceover: Now the payoff. F4 is the value help. It's the list that pops up. Users pick open, closed or rejected. Not one line of code.
slides.spoken: Now the payoff. F4 is the value help. It's the list that pops up. Users pick open, closed or rejected. Not one line of code.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Checked on *screens* only
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: thinking it guards everything. Your own UPDATE in code isn't checked. Only screen input is.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: thinking it guards everything. Your own UPDATE in code isn't checked. Only screen input is.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Fixed values = *F4 list* + check
slides.body: List the allowed values once in the domain: every screen offers them and checks them.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: list the allowed values once, in the domain. Every screen then offers them and checks them.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: list the allowed values once, in the domain. Every screen then offers them and checks them.

1. Single Vals: each allowed value plus a short description
2. F4 help shows them as a list, no code needed
3. Screen input is checked against them
4. Your own UPDATE or INSERT in code is not checked

slides.title: Stop writing *APPEND* five times
slides.subtitle: Seven-forty syntax
slides.voiceover: Stop writing APPEND five times in a row. One statement does it.
slides.spoken: Stop writing APPEND five times in a row. One statement does it.

slides.question: Fill a table in *one statement*?
slides.voiceover: Quick quiz. Which one fills a whole table in one statement? APPEND, VALUE, or INSERT? Think.
slides.spoken: Quick quiz. Which one fills a whole table in one statement? APPEND, VALUE, or INSERT? Think.

slides.heading: Answer: *VALUE #( )*
slides.code:
lt_items = VALUE #(
  ( matnr = 'MAT-01' menge = 10 )
  ( matnr = 'MAT-02' menge = 5 ) ).
slides.voiceover: It's VALUE. Each row sits in its own brackets. No work area, no APPEND. The hash sign? It takes the type from the left.
slides.spoken: It's VALUE. Each row sits in its own brackets. No work area, no APPEND. The hash sign? It takes the type from the left.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: VALUE *replaces* the table
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: using it on a filled table. VALUE wipes them first. Add BASE to keep the old rows.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: using it on a filled table. VALUE wipes them first. Add BASE to keep the old rows.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: One statement, *every row*
slides.body: VALUE #( ) builds the whole table at once. Add BASE to keep existing rows.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: VALUE builds the whole table in one statement. Add BASE when the old rows must stay.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: VALUE builds the whole table in one statement. Add BASE when the old rows must stay.

posts.caption:
Stop writing APPEND five times in a row. One statement does it.

The ABAP 7.40 VALUE operator fills an internal table inline:

1. VALUE #( ) builds the whole table in one statement
2. Each row goes in its own brackets, no work area needed
3. Careful: VALUE replaces existing rows. Add BASE to keep them

Quiz answer: VALUE #( ), available since ABAP 7.40.

Next: Part 9, intervals (today at 5 PM).

slides.title: Stop typing *12 fixed values*
slides.voiceover: Stop typing twelve fixed values for months. There's a shorter way. Last time we learned fixed values. Now, intervals.
slides.spoken: Stop typing 12 fixed values for months. There's a shorter way. Last time we learned fixed values. Now, intervals.

slides.heading: The *Intervals* block
slides.voiceover: An interval is a range of allowed values. Same Value Range tab. The Intervals block sits under Single Vals. Lower limit, zero one. Upper limit, twelve. Activate.
slides.spoken: An interval is a range of allowed values. Same Value Range tab. The Intervals block sits under Single Vals. Lower limit, 01. Upper limit, 12. Activate.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: What the screen *accepts*
slides.title: Month field, ZD_MONTH
slides.voiceover: Example. Type zero five, it's fine. Twelve, also fine. Thirteen? Rejected, it's outside.
slides.spoken: Example. Type 05, it's fine. 12, also fine. 13? Rejected, it's outside.

slides.heading: Mix *both* blocks
slides.voiceover: You can mix both blocks. Interval: zero one to twelve. Single value: zero zero, meaning not set. Either one passes the check.
slides.spoken: You can mix both blocks. Interval: 01 to 12. Single value: 00, meaning not set. Either one passes the check.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Numbers in a *CHAR* domain
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: number ranges in a CHAR domain. Text compares character by character. So five counts as bigger than twelve. Use NUMC with leading zeros.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: number ranges in a CHAR domain. Text compares character by character. So 5 counts as bigger than 12. Use NUMC with leading zeros.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Intervals = *ranges*, same check
slides.body: An interval allows every value from Lower Limit to Upper Limit. Screens check it like fixed values.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: an interval allows a whole range. Screens check it just like fixed values.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: an interval allows a whole range. Screens check it just like fixed values.

2. Mix them with single values, e.g. 00 = not set
3. Screens check them just like fixed values
4. Use NUMC, not CHAR, for number ranges

slides.title: Your value table checks *nothing*
slides.voiceover: Stop trusting your value table to check values. It checks nothing. Last time we learned intervals. Now, the value table.
slides.spoken: Stop trusting your value table to check values. It checks nothing. Last time we learned intervals. Now, the value table.

slides.heading: The *Value Table* field
slides.voiceover: Look at the standard domain LAND1, for country keys. Value Range tab, at the bottom. Value table: T005. That's SAP's table of countries.
slides.spoken: Look at the standard domain LAND1, for country keys. Value Range tab, at the bottom. Value table: T005. That's SAP's table of countries.

slides.label: HOW IT WORKS
slides.heading: From proposal to *real check*
slides.voiceover: Here's why it exists. Domain: it holds T005 as a suggestion. Field: a table field uses that domain. Foreign key: you add it in SE11, the link to the table with valid values. Check table: SE11 proposes T005. A check table is what SAP checks values against. Screen input: now it's checked.
slides.spoken: Here's why it exists. Domain: it holds T005 as a suggestion. Field: a table field uses that domain. Foreign key: you add it in SE11, the link to the table with valid values. Check table: SE11 proposes T005. A check table is what SAP checks values against. Screen input: now it's checked.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: User types *ZZ*
slides.title: Country field, typed ZZ
slides.voiceover: Example. A user types Z Z as a country. Value table only: accepted. With the foreign key: rejected.
slides.spoken: Example. A user types ZZ as a country. Value table only: accepted. With the foreign key: rejected.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Value table vs *check table*
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: mixing them up. The value table is a suggestion on the domain. The check table sits on the field. It really checks.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: mixing them up. The value table is a suggestion on the domain. The check table sits on the field. It really checks.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: Value table *proposes*, check table checks
slides.body: The value table only suggests a check table. Only a foreign key on the field makes SAP check.
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: the value table only proposes. A foreign key makes the check real.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: the value table only proposes. A foreign key makes the check real.

2. Foreign key: the link you create on a table field in SE11
3. Check table: what SAP really checks against, proposed from the value table
4. No foreign key, no check
